source: Shchekotykhin, Friedrich, Fleiss, Rodler (2012) Interactive ontology debugging: two query strategies for efficient fault localization (J. Web Semantics 12)
finding: Diagnosis of a faulty ontology gives many candidate diagnoses. The debugger asks an oracle yes/no questions about what the intended ontology entails. Entropy-based query choice, using prior fault odds, needs far fewer queries than a split-in-half rule.
numbers: Entropy method needs more than 50% fewer queries than split-in-half and random when the target diagnosis has 2 axioms (7 real ontologies, about 8 s per query). Up to 60% saving in good and average cases. Transportation ontology, bad case: 12.67 vs 13.8 queries; University bad case 6.97 vs 7 (near equal).
limits: Oracle assumed perfect. Gain shrinks when the true diagnosis gets a low prior (bad case) and when the target has more axioms. Evaluation simulated, not human.
agent_relevance: S5 REVISE: pick the next question by expected information about the fault, not by halving. Use priors, but expect little loss when priors are flat.

source: Shchekotykhin et al. (2012) stress test of the entropy debugger on large ontologies
finding: The entropy debugger worked on ontologies of over 33,000 axioms.
numbers: Target diagnosis found in 190 seconds with an average of 5 queries on an ontology of over 33,000 axioms (stress tests, Tables 12-13).
limits: Single random alteration per run; faults injected, not natural.
agent_relevance: Question-driven fault location can stay cheap on big artefacts when conflicts come from a black-box reasoner.

source: Shchekotykhin, Friedrich, Fleiss, Rodler (2010) Query strategy for sequential ontology debugging
finding: First form of the query idea: diagnoses partition by what they predict. Each query must remove at least one diagnosis whatever the answer. Minimum number of queries is log2(n) for n equally likely diagnoses; known fault odds can beat it.
numbers: Worked examples with diagnosis probabilities (e.g. posterior 0.9918 vs 0.0082 after two answers). Lower bound log2 n queries.
limits: Theory plus small examples; heavy numbers are in the 2012 journal version.
agent_relevance: Gives a code-checkable rule: ask only questions whose answers split the live hypotheses.

source: Rodler, Shchekotykhin, Fleiss, Friedrich (2012) RIO: Minimizing User Interaction in Ontology Debugging
finding: Fault priors can help or hurt. A reinforcement-style strategy (RIO) shifts between entropy and a no-risk split rule depending on how well the priors are doing.
numbers: Better vs worse of split-in-half and entropy differed by 190% to 1145% on average, maximum 2300%, across 4 ontology-matching experiments. RIO beat both on average.
limits: Ontology matching outputs; simulated oracle.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a prior blindly. Track whether the prior is paying off and fall back to a neutral rule when it is not (same idea as signal-only switching in G1).

source: Shchekotykhin, Fleiss, Rodler, Friedrich (2012) Direct computation of diagnoses for ontology debugging
finding: When an ontology has very many conflicts (ontology matching), conflict-first hitting-set search fails. Direct diagnosis computation (Inv-HS-Tree) skips conflict sets.
numbers: 146 ontologies tested with HS-Tree and Inv-HS-Tree; both finished on 133. 13 cases only the direct method solved (HS-Tree found 1 diagnosis in 2 hours on one). About 25 s per minimal diagnosis. Only 2 of 14 matching systems gave consistent and coherent alignments. Anatomy sources: 11,545 and 4,838 axioms.
limits: Two-hour limit; OAEI 2011 data.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis generator that does not need all conflicts first is the cheaper route when evidence is huge.

source: Rodler, Jannach, Schekotihin, Fleiss (2019/2022) Are Query-Based Ontology Debuggers Really Helping Knowledge Engineers? (Knowledge-Based Systems)
finding: Human studies of the OntoDebug query-based tool. Study 1: 29 CS students, test-case debugging with a diagnosis list. Study 2: 23 participants, within-subject, query-based vs test-case debugging on two SROIQ ontologies (46 sessions).
numbers: Study 1: 77% of 5 injected faults found; 10 of 29 (34%) found the full true diagnosis; 28 min, 81 clicks. Study 2: 91.3% (queries) vs 89.1% (test cases) faults found, not significant. Time 24.9 vs 34.0 min (p=0.0418, Wilcoxon). Clicks 64 vs 139 (p<0.00001). About 72% found all faults.
limits: Small samples, students, only two ontologies in Study 2. Effort gain shown, accuracy gain not shown.
agent_relevance: Interactive questioning saves effort without raising accuracy. Our agent should not claim better answers from questioning alone, only cheaper ones.

source: Rodler et al. (2019/2022) user-error findings in query-based debugging
finding: Users err when answering the system's questions and when writing test cases. Negative test cases (non-entailments) are wrong more often than positive ones. Many users did not recognise the true diagnosis even when it was shown.
numbers: 244 test cases in Study 1, 71% positive. Fault rate 24% for negative vs 10% for positive. 10 of 14 participants whose list showed the true diagnosis near the top kept testing until one diagnosis was left. Study 2: about one quarter made at least one wrong input, equal for queries and test cases. About two thirds of wrong test cases had complex class expressions.
limits: Effect measured on OWL axioms.
agent_relevance: G2/G3: an oracle or verifier can be wrong. Ask questions the oracle answers well (positive, simple). Treat a single answer as evidence, not fact.

source: Rodler et al. (2019/2022) overconfidence of debuggers
finding: Debuggers were overconfident in their own fix, and those who failed were slightly more confident than those who succeeded.
numbers: Mean confidence about 83% against 34% who located the true diagnosis (Study 1). Study 2: equal confidence with both tools.
limits: Self-report on a 0-100 scale; students.
agent_relevance: Do not use the model's own stated confidence to stop revising (G2, G5). Stop on a check.

source: Rodler (2020) On Expert Behaviors and Question Types for Efficient Query-Based Ontology Fault Localization
finding: Existing query methods assume the expert answers in a given way. A simpler interaction (different question type) works better when the expert behaves differently.
numbers: Fewer expert interactions in 66% of cases and at least 80% less expert waiting time than existing methods, on faulty real-world ontologies.
limits: Short paper; fuller numbers in IEA/AIE 2019 and the KBS journal.
agent_relevance: Match the question to who answers. An LLM oracle has its own error pattern; test it.

source: Rodler and Schmid (2018) Evaluating Active Learning Heuristics for Sequential Diagnosis (DX / RuleML)
finding: Which question-picking rule is best depends on diagnosis count, size and prior quality. No rule is always best.
numbers: A wrong rule costs average overhead of about 100% and up to 250% in oracle effort (thesis summary). Misleading priors: random choice best. Vague priors: MPS rule. Good priors: BME rule, close to entropy. Coefficients of variance of scenario columns 3% to 26%.
limits: Real ontology benchmarks; simulated oracle.
agent_relevance: Pick the question rule by how far we trust our priors. Keep a cheap random fallback.

source: Rodler and Elichanova (2020/2022) Do We Really Sample Right in Model-Based Diagnosis?
finding: Practice estimates from the few most likely diagnoses (biased best-first sample). Unbiased random samples estimate better but do not always lead to better questions.
numbers: Best-first best for ENT and SPL rules and small samples. For the MPS rule best-first needed up to over 100% more measurements: 58 vs 25 for problem U with k=50. Time vs information trade-off: the fastest sampler is not the most informative.
limits: Real knowledge-base benchmarks; simulated.
agent_relevance: A biased candidate pool can be fine for choosing the next probe. More random breadth is not always better.

source: Rodler (2020) DynamicHS: Streamlining Reiter's Hitting-Set Tree for Sequential Diagnosis
finding: Keep the search tree between questions instead of rebuilding it. Answers a question Reiter posed in 1987.
numbers: Less time than HS-Tree in 96% of sessions. Median / max time saving 52% / 75%. Hard conflict-finding calls cut by median 74%, max 99%; a hard call costs a median 19x and up to 120x an easy one. Memory under 2x HS-Tree in 82% of scenarios.
limits: Knowledge-base benchmarks only; some KB runs ended in errors.
agent_relevance: Keep state across revision rounds. Reuse earlier conflicts. Cache what failed.

source: Rodler (2020/2022) RBF-HS: Recursive Best-First Hitting Set Search (Memory-limited MBD, AIJ)
finding: A linear-memory, sound, complete, best-first diagnosis search. A hybrid, HBF-HS, trades memory for speed.
numbers: Versus HS-Tree on KB benchmarks: memory down by up to several orders of magnitude in most cases; runtime lower in over a third of minimal-cardinality cases. Most-probable-first: memory saved roughly one for one against runtime overhead.
limits: Benchmarks are knowledge bases, not software or spreadsheets.
agent_relevance: Bounded memory is possible without losing completeness, at more compute.

source: Rodler (2022) How should I compute my candidates? Taxonomy of diagnosis computation algorithms
finding: Classifies diagnosis algorithms: complete or incomplete, any-first, conflict-based or direct, black-box or glass-box. Notes diagnosis has been used for software, logic programs, recommenders, ontologies, KBs, circuits, robots, scheduling.
numbers: No experiment; taxonomy only.
limits: Abstract and intro read, class list read in DynamicHS paper.
agent_relevance: Map of design choices for the hypothesis-generation step in S5.

source: Rodler (2023) Don't Treat the Symptom, Find the Cause! Habilitation thesis (arXiv 2306.12850)
finding: A decade of MBD work from one group: speed, interactive debugging, query heuristics, spreadsheet debugging, ontology quality. States that knowledge base debugging (KBD) generalises Reiter MBD.
numbers: Rodler and Schekotihin 2017: any MBD problem reduces to a KBD problem; sequential MBD is a special case of sequential KBD.
limits: Self-reported summary of the author's own papers. Figures did not extract cleanly.
agent_relevance: One common frame: system description, observations, test cases, minimal conflicts, minimal diagnoses, queries.

source: Hofer, Jannach, Nica, Rodler, Wotawa (2022) On modeling techniques for spreadsheet debugging (read through Rodler 2023 summary)
finding: Three constraint models of a spreadsheet: exact value-based, functional-dependency (cell correct or faulty), and a new qualitative one (value too low, exact, too high). Abstract models are much faster and give a similar number of diagnoses but allow spurious ones.
numbers: Number of returned diagnoses always within one order of magnitude across model types. Abstract models up to more than four orders of magnitude faster than the value-based model. Qualitative model matched the value model in about a third of cases.
limits: Read from a thesis summary with damaged text; exact table values not verified. Original article not opened.
agent_relevance: S5: coarse high / low / ok reasoning is a cheap surrogate. Use exact values only to confirm.

source: Jannach and Schmitz (2016) Model-based diagnosis of spreadsheet programs: a constraint-based debugging approach (Automated Software Engineering 23)
finding: Core spreadsheet-diagnosis paper: formulas are components, a user-given expected value for an output cell yields conflicts, hitting sets give ranked candidate faulty cells. The 2015 fragment paper cites it as the diagnosis method to use.
numbers: No numbers verified; page blocked by a redirect.
limits: Not opened. Pointer only.
agent_relevance: Cell-as-component mapping is the template for turning any artefact into a diagnosable model.

source: Jannach and Schmitz (2015) Using Calculation Fragments for Spreadsheet Testing and Debugging
finding: Users often cannot give expected values for big spreadsheets. Proposal: auto-cut the sheet into small overlapping fragments the user can check, then run MBD per fragment.
numbers: Position paper, 4 pages, no evaluation.
limits: Conjecture only that small fragments speed up fault finding.
agent_relevance: Shrink the object under test until a check is easy, like unit-testing a piece before the whole.

source: Ayalew and Mittermeir (2008) Spreadsheet Debugging (EuSpRIG)
finding: Pre-MBD fault tracing in spreadsheets from interval-based testing: use dataflow and cell marks to find the most influential faulty cell behind a propagated fault.
numbers: No large experiment read in the part opened.
limits: Skimmed abstract and intro only.
agent_relevance: Baseline non-diagnosis method: trace backward along data flow.

source: Lambrix (2019/2020) Completing and Debugging Ontologies: State of the Art and Challenges
finding: Frames ontology repair as abduction: choose add and delete sets under preferences (minimal, skyline-optimal, more complete, less incorrect). Notes oracle-per-axiom repair as a natural step.
numbers: Survey, no experiments.
limits: Abstract and definitions read.
agent_relevance: Repair is a separate choice from locating the fault; keep both steps apart in S5.

source: Singha et al. (2025) Benchmark Dataset Generation and Evaluation for Excel Formula Repair with LLMs (FoRepBench, KDD 2025 workshop)
finding: Microsoft built a 618-sample benchmark of broken Excel formulas (5 runtime error types such as #DIV/0!) by synthetic expansion of forum seeds, with LLM-as-judge and execution checks. A context-aware LLM repair baseline is tested.
numbers: Execution match on FoRepBench: GPT-4.1 0.80, GPT-4o 0.73, Phi-3 0.58, Mistral 0.51. Can-execute: 0.96, 0.93, 0.77, 0.76. Syntax-valid: 1.00, 1.00, 0.81, 0.78.
limits: Synthetic data is easier than real forum cases (next line). One repair attempt, no diagnosis step.
agent_relevance: Plain LLM repair of formulas is good on simple faults. No hypothesis ranking is used.

source: Singha et al. (2025) FoRepBench seed-set gap
finding: On the real forum seed samples the same models do far worse than on the synthetic set.
numbers: Execution match on seed set: GPT-4.1 0.41, GPT-4o 0.35, Phi-3 0.24, Mistral 0.19 (vs 0.80, 0.73, 0.58, 0.51 on FoRepBench). Can-execute 0.65, 0.63, 0.41, 0.37. Human annotation on 24 samples.
limits: Seed set small, from the MrExcel forum. Synthetic samples are less nested and less ambiguous.
agent_relevance: Benchmarks made by LLMs overstate skill. Measure on real faults (G3).

source: Zhu et al. (2026) SpreadsheetBench 2: evaluating agents on end-to-end business spreadsheet workflows
finding: 321 expert-checked tasks over multi-sheet workbooks (generation, debugging, visualization). 100 are debugging tasks where the instruction only says audit and fix; error location is not given. Eight frontier LLMs in one multi-turn agent scaffold.
numbers: Best model overall 34.89%. Debugging best 12% (Claude Opus 4.6). Visualization best 62.5%. Average 11.8 sheets and 593.5 modified cells per task; debugging 656.6 cells. Hardest debug type is explicit error values (#REF!, #NUM!), best barely above 20%. Spreadsheet products: Claude for Excel best at 15.4% on a 30-task subset.
limits: Whole-workbook match scoring is strict.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that unaided LLMs fail at fault localization on real artefacts. This gap is what a diagnosis scaffold targets.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) SpreadsheetBench 2 failure analysis
finding: Manual review of failed Claude Opus 4.6 runs: main causes are insufficient inspection and wrong target-cell choice. On debugging, two models spent over 60% of steps inspecting.
numbers: Failure taxonomy of six modes; Turn Limit Exceeded 3.4%, Format/Output error 4.7%. Stronger models gained from more reliable steps, not larger interaction budgets.
limits: Single model's failures sampled by hand.
agent_relevance: Localization, not repair, is the bottleneck. Code should enumerate candidate cells and force a check on each (G2).

source: Reiter (1987) A theory of diagnosis from first principles (Artificial Intelligence 32)
finding: Foundation: a diagnosis is a minimal set of components assumed abnormal that restores consistency with observations, computed as minimal hitting sets of conflict sets via the HS-Tree.
numbers: Not opened. DynamicHS paper says Reiter asked in 1987 whether a tree could be reused across iterations.
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: Defines the hypothesis-and-conflict machinery all the work above builds on.

source: Felfernig, Friedrich, Jannach, Stumptner (2004) Consistency-based diagnosis of configuration knowledge bases (Artificial Intelligence 152(2):213-234)
finding: Applied consistency-based diagnosis to debugging configuration knowledge bases using test cases; citation confirmed in the reference list of Rodler's papers.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers.
limits: Only the citation line was read.
agent_relevance: Test cases act as observations that expose a faulty rule, like our held-out check.

source: Junker (2004) QuickXPlain (AAAI); plain explanation by Rodler (2020) arXiv 2001.01835
finding: Divide-and-conquer minimal conflict finder; black-box. Rodler 2020 gives a plain explanation and proof.
numbers: Not opened.
limits: Secondhand via reference lists.
agent_relevance: A cheap way to shrink a failing set of assumptions to a minimal conflict using only yes/no checks.

source: Rodler and Schekotihin (2017) Reducing model-based diagnosis to knowledge base debugging (DX)
finding: Proof that the KBD problem generalises Reiter MBD. Sequential KBD lets the user give more kinds of measurements (entailed and not entailed).
numbers: Theorem-level result; no numbers.
limits: Read as thesis summary only.
agent_relevance: Supports using one debugging frame for software, spreadsheets and KBs.
